articles.title: North Korean IT Workers Infiltrate US Tech Jobs
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox IT worker scams are a primary method of funding Pyongyang’s weapons programme, alongside thefts of cryptocurrency. PHOTO: AFP Dustin Volz Published Oct 14, 2026, 09:25 AM Updated Oct 14, 2026, 10:08 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise The FBI disrupted a North Korean IT job network that used US facilitators and laptop farms to fund Pyongyang’s nuclear and ballistic weapons programmes. US officials said more than 40 laptop farms were dismantled in Texas, nearly 200 devices were seized, and indictments were unsealed against 12 suspects over a US$3 million fraud. The scheme used stolen identities, AI tools and Western accomplices to trick US firms, and the FBI warned the threat is growing and highly serious. AI generated WASHINGTON – The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) in September disrupted a widespread network of American facilitators accused of aiding the North Korean government in securing remote information technology jobs that helped fund the reclusive country’s nuclear and ballistic weapons programmes, US officials said Oct 13. The operation included the dismantling of more than 40 so-called laptop farms across Texas and the seizure of nearly 200 computer devices, the officials said, marking one of the largest efforts to date by the US authorities to block a key revenue stream that has helped North Korea evade harsh international sanctions and generate billions in cash in recent years. The Justice Department separately unsealed indictments in Ohio on Oct 13 against two US nationals and 10 China-based North Koreans accused of committing identity theft to earn pay cheques from unwitting US companies that hired them. Prosecutors said that scheme bilked 70 companies out of more than US$3 million (S$3.84 million) and ran from 2019 to 2025. The identities of two additional defendants remained under seal. The moves were the latest by the US in an intensifying campaign to try to cut off a stealthy and evolving digital threat from North Korea whose scale is not entirely clear but likely vast. US intelligence officials in the Biden and second Trump administrations have said the information technology worker scams are a primary method of funding Pyongyang’s weapons programme, alongside thefts of cryptocurrency. North Korea is deploying “thousands of state-controlled IT workers to infiltrate companies in the United States and allied countries”, Brett Leatherman, the head of the FBI’s cyber division, said in an interview. “Every one of these jobs is funding a stream for a nuclear and ballistic missiles programme obtained with the stolen identity of an American and the trust of an American employer.” The bureau worked closely with the US-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike to identify and disrupt the network, Leatherman said. He added that the coordinated actions were an early example of the FBI’s new cyber strategy, which was unveiled in September and promised closer collaboration with the private sector to target hackers in ways that impede or thwart malicious activity. The strategy is part of a broader effort across the Trump administration to work more closely with US companies to strike hackers with cyberattacks, a pivot cautiously welcomed by some security experts. US officials and cybersecurity analysts have said the North Korean IT worker scheme is among the most serious ongoing digital threats facing businesses today and that it remains underappreciated as a risk. Adam Meyers, who oversees counter-adversary operations at CrowdStrike, said the North Korean schemes to get hired for jobs have been “increasing both in prevalence and complexity”. It is difficult to know how widespread laptop farms are in the US, Meyers said, but noted that CrowdStrike identified an average of two new cases per day throughout September – which is likely only the tip of the iceberg. For more than two years, US intelligence officials and cybersecurity researchers have warned that North Korea has been using stolen American identities – often acquired from compromised private information, like Social Security numbers, on the dark web – and artificial intelligence tools to get hired for remote IT jobs at companies across the US, Europe and elsewhere. Experts have said companies ranging from small start-ups to Fortune 500 firms have been victimised. A crucial aspect of the fraud campaign is support from people in the US who are recruited by North Korea to help bypass corporate security measures that detect fraudulent hires, according to investigators. Facilitators help enable the fraud by receiving and setting up work laptops at addresses that appear like legitimate residences to corporate human resources teams. North Korean operators then use software to remotely tunnel into those laptops and work on them, posing as Americans to the companies that hired them. The appeal for facilitators is simple: Jobs that look like easy cash and, at least at first, might not require much of them. “They get kind of hooked on it initially, and then more gets asked of them, and they’re kind of in too deep at that point,” Meyers said. Leatherman said that the Texas sweep did not include any arrests of facilitators but that the authorities warned them they could face criminal penalties should they continue to assist with remote fraud. The decision stemmed in part from a desire to move quickly to upend the network rather than wait for prosecutors to file charges, he said. Leatherman said the laptop farms often operate like a “mini data centre” for the North Koreans, where one facilitator hosts dozens or even hundreds of laptops used to fill scores of jobs. A woman in Arizona sentenced in 2025 to more than eight years in prison was accused of hosting dozens of laptops at her home to help North Koreans connect to more than 300 US companies. The tactics of North Korea’s IT worker army have steadily evolved to evade detection. That includes increased reliance on artificial intelligence to create fake resumes, videos and photos, and to navigate virtual job interviews, officials said. The fraudsters are also relying more on sub-contractors in places like Pakistan and Nigeria to further obscure North Korean involvement, Leatherman said. In an advisory released on Oct 13, the FBI said the North Koreans were paying Americans and other Western accomplices to “perform a growing variety of identity and location obfuscation tasks” that included appearing on camera, participating in job interviews or meetings, verifying fraudulent identities, shipping packages, and even completing urinalysis tests or fingerprint submissions. articles.title: OpenAI Employee Arrested for Conference Room Bugging
articles.content: Image source, US Department of JusticeImage caption, Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee. Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product. Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say. On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said. OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier". According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment. Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'". Image source, US Department of JusticeImage caption, The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene. That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said. Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation. If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000). articles.title: Microsoft Plans Multi-Gigawatt AI Accelerator Rollout
articles.content: 96-chip configuration promises seven times its predecessor's token throughput, with production deployments due in 2027 Dan Robinson Dan Robinson IT INFRASTRUCTURE REPORTER Published tue 13 Oct 2026 // 14:30 UTC Make us preferred on Google Anthropic reinvents source control as Claude floods the world with code 3 hours ago OpenAI's dot assistant burned 300K+ tokens in a day without a single prompt 5 hours ago Apple unleashes a swarm of Mac Minions to share GPU resources for large AI tasks 6 hours ago Anthropic conjures another threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse 9 hours ago Cheap Chinese and open source LLMs could trigger trillion-dollar AI infrastructure 'reset' 9 hours ago Microsoft has lifted the lid on the next generation of its Azure Maia custom AI chips, saying it will usher in a new phase of its compute infrastructure where everything is closely integrated to meet the demands of agentic inference. The Redmond giant says its Azure Maia 200, announced earlier this year , is now serving production workloads and that a successor is already planned for 2027. Azure Maia 300 is described as "a complete intelligent system" designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today. Microsoft claims a full 96-accelerator configuration will deliver up to seven times Maia 200's rack-scale token throughput, while offering 40 percent more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. Its next-gen chip is created with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads, according to a blog post by Microsoft's EVP for Cloud and AI, Scott Guthrie. The firm envisions it being deployed in rack-scale systems comprising up to 96 accelerators, while each Maia 300 will feature eight HBM4 memory stacks providing up to 18 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth, the better to support execution of large models and long-context workloads. This sounds similar to the kind of rack-scale AI equipment that has already been developed by Nvidia for its GPU accelerators , and more recently by AMD with its Helion and Helios infrastructure, all designed to make the most of their own specific silicon and software stacks. Microsoft says that Maia 300 is "built as a complete system, with software, silicon, physical rack infrastructure, networking, and datacenters co-designed to operate as a single platform to meet the demands of cloud-scale agentic inference." It insists that this system-level approach is necessary for agentic workloads, which involve multi-step execution, long-context decoding and tool use, and "change the computational profile and arithmetic intensity of inference." The growing emphasis on in-house integration contrasts with Microsoft's 2024 "AI Access Principles," which stressed partnerships across its technology stack. The firm even complained to the European Commission's competition authorities that Google had a competitive advantage because of its approach. "Only one company – Google," said Microsoft at the time, "is vertically integrated in a manner that provides it with strength and independence at every AI layer from chips to a thriving mobile app store. Everybody else must rely on partnerships to innovate and compete." Microsoft now has its own AI chips, rack-scale designs, and internally developed MAI models , giving it more control over its stack. It plans to scale Azure Maia to "multi-gigawatt deployments" starting in 2027. We asked Microsoft for comment. Guthrie said that the firm will share more details on its strategy at next month's Microsoft Ignite 2026 event in San Francisco. ® microsoft ai and ml systems azure Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Anthropic Floods World with Claude, Reinvents Code Control
articles.content: When continuous integration gits you down, there's always an AI-tuned monorepo Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published tue 13 Oct 2026 // 23:37 UTC Make us preferred on Google OpenAI's dot assistant burned 300K+ tokens in a day without a single prompt 5 hours ago Apple unleashes a swarm of Mac Minions to share GPU resources for large AI tasks 6 hours ago Claude submitted fake murder tip to Philly police during summertime testing 8 hours ago Anthropic conjures another threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse 9 hours ago Cheap Chinese and open source LLMs could trigger trillion-dollar AI infrastructure 'reset' 9 hours ago Anthropic's Claude models have been emitting so much code that the company's coding infrastructure hasn't been able to keep up. It's a symptom of the AI coding imperative and all-you-can-eat inference. Microsoft's GitHub in April published a blog post attributing recent availability problems to the exponential growth in pull requests and commits. The code flood has been noted by academic researchers, among others. For Anthropic, writing code is no longer a productivity bottleneck. Instead, the problem is managing the code after it's written, via source control, the build system, and continuous integration. "In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day," the biz said in a blog post on Tuesday. "We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce." After several months of model prompting and five months of migration, the result is a homemade version control system called Scion, a monorepo scheme that sounds a bit like Subversion, Apache's centralized version control system. Anthropic is not the first organization to look beyond Git's distributed architecture toward centralized source control. Google uses Piper , a monorepo system (along with Gerrit for Git-based code reviews). Microsoft has Virtual File System for Git, formerly GVFS , to help overcome some of the scaling issues with Git. Meta has Sapling . But as the AI biz notes, Claude's code writing ability both created the situation and offered a way out through the creation of scalable code infrastructure tools – in addition to Scion, Claude helped conjure Antique (a code review interface), a code search tool, and a source control IAM system. The decentralized approach embodied by Git is the right one for most code repos, according to Anthropic. But the company's main branch weighs in at about 100 GB, with a compressed working copy at more than a quarter of that. "We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs," Anthropic said. "Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day." Even with the tools Git provides for working with portions of a codebase, Anthropic says operations proved challenging. Scion has been designed to meet the needs of AI agents, so the client leaves much of the work to the server; the source control queries are exposed via API so internal tools can respond without needing a local repo, and there's less synchronization but more need for server speed. "In Scion, the unit of work is a 'changeset,' an entry in a write-ahead log," Anthropic explains. "A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage." Work on Scion started in January, and when Claude Mythos Preview became available internally, Anthropic's code coaxers told the model to rewrite an early Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline. articles.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Call for AI Regulation in UK
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta , both of which declined to back new legislation. The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework . The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.” OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said. However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.” The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.” While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI. MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said. In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over. Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said. When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so. “What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.” The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government , we will continue to do it.” . The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.” Geoffrey Irving said the labs believe they are locked in a race that governments will not interrupt and that they cannot leave. “Both of those are false,” he said. “They could just stop.” Following the hearing Byrne told WIRED that his committee would now dedicate a lot of time examining the UK’s path forward as a middle power on AI. He wants ministers to use Britain’s coming G20 presidency, alongside South Korea, which follows it in the chair, to broker an international convention that does not depend on the current White House. “The G20 presidency will outlive the US presidency of Trump,” he said. “The risks,” he added, “are multiplying faster than our safety regime can control.”

articles.title: MI5 Chief Warns of Threats from Russia, Iran, and AI
articles.content: Watch: State threats and AI - Key takeaways from MI5 chief's speech MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said. Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases. At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders". He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones. He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons. However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years. Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly". Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks. "With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said. "So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding." He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand." His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved". He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute". He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference. "I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sir Ken McCallum gave his annual address at MI5's headquarters in central London Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK. The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities. Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites". Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique". He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK." The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police. Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard". The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response." Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia. On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual. "We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist." Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes". "These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on." Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are". He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities". In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely. Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism. He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent." Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK". He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

articles.content: Kroger laying off 3,000 corporate employees over 3 years amid increased AI use by The Associated Press - 10/13/26 12:37 PM ET Link copied Link copied NOW PLAYING Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations. “Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.” Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.” Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer. Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO. Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities. Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells. Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon. Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed. A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value. Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee. Kroger shares fell 1.6% in morning trading Tuesday, to $61.66. articles.title: US Military Veteran EHR Modernization Hits $17B Boost
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Edward Graham , Managing Editor, Nextgov/FCW | October 13, 2026 04:58 PM ET The ranking members of the House and Senate Veterans’ Affairs committees said VA’s “citation of ‘unanticipated complexities’ as the rationale for nearly tripling the original contract remains unexplained.” Congress Veterans Affairs Health Records The top Democrats on the House and Senate panels overseeing the Department of Veterans Affairs are pressing the agency to disclose the rationale behind its recent decision to boost its electronic health record modernization contract with Oracle Health by $17 billion. In an Oct. 6-dated letter to VA Secretary Doug Collins that was publicly released on Tuesday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Rep. Mark Takano, D-Calif., said they had “serious concerns” about the agency’s “lack of transparency and cooperation” with Congress when it comes to oversight of the EHR overhaul and contract extension. Blumenthal is ranking member of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, while Takano is ranking member of the House veterans panel. The letter was first reported on Tuesday by Bloomberg Government. VA announced in August that it was extending its current 10-year, $10 billion modernization deal with Oracle to include an additional $17 billion ceiling and three one-year option periods. That decision was quietly disclosed in an award notice posted at the time on SAM.gov — a move that surprised lawmakers from both parties. The extension also followed extensive issues VA and Oracle have faced implementing the new EHR system across the agency’s nationwide network of 164 medical facilities, which has faced usability issues, technical glitches and patient safety issues since the first software go-live at Mann-Grandstaff VA Medical Center in Spokane, Washington, in 2020. In their letter, Blumenthal and Takano said “VA’s citation of ‘unanticipated complexities’ as the rationale for nearly tripling the original contract remains unexplained.” During a House Veterans’ Affairs Committee hearing last month, Democrat and Republican members alike lambasted VA’s massive contract extension with Oracle Health and voted 19-0 to subpoena Oracle Chairman and Co-founder Larry Ellison and Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia to appear before the panel to discuss the project’s cost and status. VA restarted full-scale deployments of the Oracle Health EHR system earlier this year after it froze most rollouts of the new software in April 2023 to address the issues plaguing the project. The agency has implemented the new EHR system at 11 VA medical facilities so far in 2026, with plans to complete two additional deployments at facilities in Alaska and Ohio before the end of the year. Agency officials have expressed their intent to rapidly accelerate EHR software go-lives on an annual basis, with plans to finalize all deployments in 2031. Blumenthal and Takano wrote that VA did not respond to an Aug. 27 request from the House VA panel to provide lawmakers with additional information on the Oracle Health EHR contract modification, including all relevant communications between VA and the company and “documentation sufficient to explain the need for the increase, including detailed descriptions of the ‘unanticipated complexities,’ and any related cost analysis or determination, including, but not limited to, the price negotiation memorandum.” In addition to requesting that delayed information, the lawmakers also asked VA to provide written responses to 13 questions about the contract extension process, including how the agency arrived at the new $27 billion total contract ceiling and whether officials will commit to obtaining a third-party total lifecycle cost estimate for the project. As Nextgov/FCW reported last year, current and former VA officials have also said the EHR software is not compliant with federal accessibility requirements mandated under Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act. Blumenthal and Takano asked VA to detail whether it was aware when it signed its initial contract that the software was not Section 508 compliant, as well as the agency’s plan to address the EHR system’s lack of 508 compliance. articles.title: Tech Icon Meg Whitman Shapes Albertsons Future
articles.content: It’s never a good sign when a company pulls its financial forecasts mid-turnaround. Recommended Video But Albertsons did just that on Tuesday in the first clear sign of how deeply newly appointed executive chair Meg Whitman plans to overhaul the struggling grocery chain. Albertsons—which, in addition to its namesake stores, operates another 21 chains including Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Tom Thumb, and Randalls—said that net sales slipped to $18.9 billion in its second fiscal quarter, led by a 0.8% drop in identical sales, a metric that strips out newly closed or open stores. It was the second quarterly drop in a row, following shrinking growth in the preceding quarter. Albertsons CEO Susan Morris announced a plan in July called “ACI Edge,” aimed at improving the company’s competitiveness by reviewing its strategy, cost structure, operations, and portfolio of brands. On Tuesday, the company said it was pulling its financial forecasts until that review is over. That suggests that Albertsons may be eyeing a deeper turnaround than initially planned under Whitman, the longtime tech executive who joined Albertsons last month. “Everything should be on the table,” Whitman told Wall Street analysts on Albertsons’ quarterly conference call. “Dramatic improvement is needed now. Albertsons must move faster to change the trajectory of the business.” Like all grocers, Albertsons has been struggling with cash-strapped shoppers burdened by food inflation and higher gas prices cutting into their spending on nonessentials. But Albertsons also has a cost structure higher than that of its rivals, leaving less room to maneuver and shield consumers from higher prices than discount grocers like Walmart and Kroger or bulk operators like Sam’s Club and Costco. While Whitman has no grocery experience and little retail experience (from her time as CEO of eBay), she was brought in by Albertsons for her turnaround chops and decisiveness. After taking the reins at Hewlett-Packard in 2011, she would go on to simplify the structure and product portfolio of a company that had been damaged by its acquisition of Autonomy Corp.; was doing strategy flip-flops; and had suffered from declining revenue and margins. She oversaw the split of the company into two. Before that, she had been CEO of eBay, where she professionalized the management structure and operations of a hot tech startup, setting it up for a period of fast growth under her decade of management. The current period of food inflation has been particularly bruising for Albertsons. Its lower-income customers are trading down to less expensive items and store brands, which either pinches Albertsons’ margins or sends shoppers to Walmart and Kroger. “The reality right now is that the economy is tough for many of our customers,” Morris said. But Albertsons’ sprawling empire of store chains has led to complex operations and the higher costs that come with them, making it harder to be more flexible on pricing. Calling Albertsons’ prices “ridiculously high compared to rivals,” GlobalData managing director Neil Saunders said that would “be partly justifiable if other dimensions—store experience, service, private label, and so forth—were above par, but they’re not.” To remedy that, he added, Albertsons would need to “invest in prices”—retail speak for “lower them.” And that in turn adds pressure to find cost savings. Whitman’s comments to analysts suggest there will be no sacred cows under her aegis. She hinted that Albertsons could shed some brands through “potential strategic actions.” Morris became CEO in 2025 after the collapse a few months earlier of the planned $24 billion Albertsons and Kroger merger was followed by the exit of both companies’ chiefs. (Albertsons is currently suing Kroger for $9 billion over the failure of the merger.) She had been operations chief for seven years. Before Whitman’s appointment, Morris had already made some moves to make Albertsons more flexible, including lowering the number of operating regions to four from 11 to generate economies of scale and speed up decision-making. She also centralized much of Albertsons’ merchandising decisions under one team. As executive chair rather than simply chair, Whitman’s role is much more hands-on, acting as a close operations and strategic advisor to Morris and helping leadership sharpen strategy, improve execution, and act with celerity. “The company has greater potential than its results have reflected,” Whitman said. “But dramatic improvement is needed now. articles.title: Sam's Club CEO Sees Power in Investing in People
articles.content: Sam’s Club CEO Latriece Watkins has a career resume that most workers would gawk at, working her way up from an intern at Walmart all the way to leader of one of America’s biggest grocery retailers. Recommended Video But it isn’t the executive titles or career milestones that makes her feel powerful: The greatest source of power comes from watching the peers she’s helped ultimately succeed. “When I feel most powerful is when I see the people I’ve invested in make moves,” Watkins told Most Powerful Women Editor Emma Hinchliffe onstage at Fortune ’s annual MPW Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., on Tuesday. “When I see them get promoted, I see all of their faces running across memory from very early in my career, or very early in their careers, to where they’ve moved now.” Solely focusing on one’s own career could leave opportunities for greater impact on the table, according to the Fortune 500 executive. Watkins has made many strides in her own career, becoming the first woman and person of color to serve as Walmart’s chief merchant back in 2023—one of the most influential roles in retail. And in helping others along her three-decade career at the $890 billion parent company (Walmart), she’s leveraged a symbiotic strategy with her peers so that everyone succeeds. “The contributions we make are more than we could individually do,” she continued. “So power for me is the names of all the people that I can say who [have] benefited from my contributions, and I’ve benefited from being able to either contribute or get feedback from them.” Watkins said that despite being in the top role, business leaders will always need people—and finding the best way to shepherd them can be a challenge for busy executives. In her eight months as CEO, the 51-year-old has found that understanding the power of workers and delivering clarity are required in leadership. Employees will be looking to the top boss for transparency and a clear vision. To get that clarity, Watkins recommends setting aside time to think things through. “People look to you for clarity, which means you have to be clear. You don’t think out loud,” she said. “When you’re the leader, people want to know what you think, and if you haven’t cleared it up for yourself and you’re thinking out loud, you’ll confuse them.” “So take the time—make the time—to create clarity for yourself,” Watkins continued. “It’s one of the hardest things to find this time for yourself. But it’s required, because you can’t get clarity without it.” Fortune Daily breaks the traditional barrier between audience and newsroom. articles.title: UK CFOs Expect AI to Cut Half of British Firm Headcounts
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox Deloitte said on Oct 14 that 52% of CFOs expect to cut headcount due to the technology, with AI adoption still in its early stages. PHOTO: AFP Published Oct 14, 2026, 08:20 AM Updated Oct 14, 2026, 09:05 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise 52% of UK CFOs expect AI to cut headcount, according to Deloitte. Most say AI is still early, with only a quarter of planned change achieved. The trend adds to Britain’s jobless growth and rising youth unemployment, creating pressure for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government and AI Minister Kanishka Narayan. A Multiverse report says firms are buying AI tools without enough worker training. It warns spend may be wasted, while only a third of CFOs expect higher margins next year. AI generated LONDON - Many of Britain’s large businesses are ready to replace staff with artificial intelligence over the next year, according to a prominent survey of chief financial officers. Deloitte said on Oct 14 that 52% of CFOs expect to cut headcount due to the technology, with AI adoption still in its early stages. More than two thirds – 67% – said they have achieved just a quarter of the changes they ultimately expect from AI. The report adds to evidence of Britain’s jobless growth revival , which poses a political dilemma for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government. AI adoption and high employment costs are encouraging firms to expand with fewer roles. As a result, long-term unemployment is rising and youth joblessness is at its highest in over a decade – an anomaly in an economy that is whizzing past European peers. It underscores the challenge facing AI Minister Kanishka Narayan, who pledged to “never leave working people to bear the cost” of the AI revolution, in a speech on Oct 12. “I understand why people are naturally anxious about their jobs and what artificial intelligence means for their children’s future,” Narayan said. “I feel that concern, that anxiety too.” While firms are using AI to cut costs, the impact on profits is less certain. Only a third of CFOs believe AI will help increase margins in the next year, according to the Deloitte report. Deloitte surveyed 66 CFOs between Sept 17 and Oct 1. Of those, 12 were from FTSE 100 companies and 25 from FTSE 250 companies. A separate report published this week by Multiverse, the London-based training platform founded by Euan Blair, suggested firms are struggling to join up AI investments with their existing workers. “Almost none of them know what their people can do with AI, and that is where their spend is going to waste,” Blair said. The report said firms are spending more on AI tools without training their workers how to use them. BLOOMBERG AI/artificial intelligence Employment Job cuts

articles.title: Tesla's 'Security Protocols' Block DHS Tracking Device
articles.content: • · Oct 13, 2026 at 10:51 AM A federal warrant application detailed how Tesla’s security protocols stopped agents from tracking a suspected drug trafficker’s car. This article was produced in collaboration with Court Watch , an independent outlet that unearths overlooked court records. Subscribe to them here . The “security protocols” on a Tesla stopped a Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agent from placing a tracking device on it, according to a warrant reviewed by 404 Media. On Halloween of 2025, an HSI Special Agent filed a more than 60 page application to place a tracking device on the Tesla of a suspected drug trafficker in Milwaukee. Agents had been watching alleged drug dealer Sam Stair — a local landlord they believed was using his rental properties as the front for a drug trafficking operation — for months when they asked a judge to let them install a tracker on his car. According to the warrant application, Stair went everywhere in a white Tesla and the agents wanted to see where it was when they couldn’t keep eyes on it. “Case agents believed that Stair is using the Tesla to assist with drug trafficking and traveling to locations associated with the DTO [drug trafficking organization] and DTO members,” the application said. “Case agents are still attempting to identify other locations used by the DTO, other members of the DTO, and the source of supply for narcotics and believe that the court order would be beneficial for the investigation.” A judge issued the warrant the same day the application was filed, but agents never got the tracking device on the car. “Search warrant not executed due to security protocols active on Tesla,” the agent said in a court filing about the warrant. The court documents don’t elaborate on the specific “security protocols” that stopped them from placing a tracking device on the car, but the Tesla may have been in “Sentry Mode.” Teslas have eight external cameras that provide a 360 degree view of the car’s surroundings. This makes the car’s self-driving features possible but also allows owners to keep track of what’s going on around the car. If a stranger approaches a Tesla while it’s in Sentry Mode, the car will flash its lights, sound an alarm, and start recording through its exterior cameras. The car’s dashboard activates and lets people outside know that Sentry Mode is active and that they’re being recorded. When the cameras start rolling, the car pings the owner via the Tesla phone app and they can watch what’s happening around their car remotely. If they’ve installed a USB drive in the car they can even save the footage. The setback didn’t matter for the long-term investigation. A task force arrested Stair and 17 other people in May on drug trafficking charges . Stair pleaded not guilty and was released from jail on bond while he awaits trial .  Matthew Gault is a writer covering weird tech, nuclear war, and video games. He’s worked for Reuters, Motherboard, and the New York Times. More from Matthew Gault • •

articles.title: Hacker News User Floods Website with AI Bot Traffic
articles.content: For the past few years, I've been working on sprinklz.io, a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed. A month ago, I posted it to HN, and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then… My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse several days after my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load. So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!). Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one specific user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked. Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc. The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that can day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users. P.S. if you'd like to check it out, the website is fully free, and available here The TLDR is that it lets you define your own customizations, in addition to things like the points totals from hacker news. You can use it to filter out topics, like AI or LLMs, but the topics are completely arbitrary and you can program your own customizations. When I tell people about the emacs web browser, their first reaction is 'Wait emacs has a web browser?!', followed by, 'yeah… I guess that's kind of a web browser'. The emacs web browser is designed to render webpages in a terminal-based, textonly environment and, well, it goes about exactly the way you'd expect. It works well on HTML-only, small-content websites, but not so good for anything else. The problem is that emacs is primarily a text-only editor, but the modern internet is very much not plain-text based. Simple HTML, designed in the simple style of the 1990s has a clear translation into plain text, but modern UI design, with it's visual styling, heavy javascript, and just, overall chaos, not so much. The emacs web browser would be great, if only we could find a way to go back in time… Ok, so the plan is simple. We take modern webpages, rewrite their source code into old-school simply-styled HTML, and then pipe it through to the emacs web browser. We just need to find a way to do this easily and at scale. So um, you didn't forget about LLMs did you? It's nice to be using them in a way that will hopefully reduce the amount of spam content in the world. Yeah, and so, I've been using it, and it runs very well. Like realistically I can use this on many webpages where eww (emacs web wowser) did not run previously. It takes a moment to generate the initial modifier program, but once it's generated, it runs pretty fast, and during day-to-day browsing, it mostly doesn't need any extra LLM calls. I have been using it myself and enjoying the experience. The source code lives here: https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb and is open-source, and free to install, etc., etc. I think we all know the answer to this: bad incentives. Technology makes systems more productive, but it does not, in fact, make you in particular more productive. The tools that enable computers to be more efficient also enable people to be more efficient at exploiting your time, attention, and wellbeing. I'm talking neural nets babyyy. I first noticed the problem in 2018. Or rather, I noticed that I had a problem, and that problem was spendinng 3 hours a day watching starcraft 2 replays and wondering where the time went, and how I managed to stay up til 2am again. What's interesting to me is that I didn't have any of these problems until the late 2010s. I had a computer with an internet connection since at least the mid 2000s, and a smartphone with twitter and reddit and the like not long after. It's possible that I've gotten less resiliant over the years, but I have a sneaking suspiscion that it's the computers who changed. I can't quite put my finger on it, but I have this sensation that every time I interact with a system or website, I'm playing this kind of adversarial game, where I'm trying to just go about my day, and maybe read a little article about computers, and they're trying to figure out a way to keep me on their site for just a little bit longer. I also have this feeling that as software engineering has moved from a discipline of hobbyists and enthusiasts to leaders who increasingly developed through finance or business-minded tracks, we've found ourselves with these major tools that we used to love become both extremely bland and extremely profitable. editor's note: I've been working on a free customizable news reader as a way to take out some of my frustrations with the modern internet. if you don't use this one, I recommend following individual blogs and websites, because it's so much better to just get off these big platforms entirely. editors note 2: i haven't yet posted this latest article to my rss xml, because i'm not ready to send notifications for it yet. will add in the coming weeks. Now that deft 0.2.0 is released, I figure it's a good time to talk about what I built, and why I built it. The point of Clojure's everything-is-a-map toolkit is that getters and setters are a waste of time. Clojure was built, in large part, in response to the crappy 2008 Java workflow, where you had to write getters, setters, and builders, and you took on all this bloat that nobody enjoyed. The problem is that if you want to represent your data using the built-in defprotocol and defrecord, and you want to define functions that depend on the presence of a certain field, then the only way to encode that information into the protocol is to add getter and setter metohds to it. icky. You can also use a combination of protocol + malli schema to represent this, but then when you use it, you need to specify 'this function takes as input something that both implements this protocol and implements this Malli schema'. Also icky. What we want is something we can use in the style of defprotocol and defrecord, but gives us all the getters and setters and map-like stuff by default. The key insight is that if a field exists in a record, we get all the other good stuff, so we just need to add support for protocols with required keys. Deft v0.2.0 adds support for namespaced keys in type and protocol definitions. i.e., you can now do: (defp Positioned :required-keys [::pos - ::Point]) and (deft Circle [::location/position radius]) (>Circle ::location/position [1 2] :radius 12) this is useful because you can now define methods that depend on those fields being present i.e.: (defp Gremlin :extends [location/Positioned]) (defmethod game-object/get-hitbox ::Gremlin [self] (js/Matter.Bodies.rectangle (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/x]) (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/y]) 15 15)) Check it out! I finished reading On the Edge last week, and it was bad. Not that I don't respect Nate Silver. I respect him a lot. So when his seminal text on gambling and risk taking was a rambling mess, I was suprised and disappointed. Nevertheless, a completionist at heart, I trudged on, to the very end, where I was greeted with this message: "ChatGPT was a significant help in writing this book, serving as a creative muse when coming up with things like chapter subheadings, metaphors, and analogies, and for refining my understanding of technical topics that are likely to be well represented in its corpus." Technically he wrote the book by hand, and technically he typed the letters onto his keyboard, but you know, did he really? Did he put his whole thought and mind and being into every word on the page? Maybe. I'm reminded of the absolute classic [Simple Made Easy](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SxdOUGdseq4), a video where so much of the core lecture is built on defining precise language, and saying exactly what you mean. When you offload that work, you don't just skip word choices, you skip that thinking, and you miss out on that organization and mental clarity. In reading Nate's book, there's a real and noticeable difference between the language that feels baked into the organizational fabric of Nate's mentality, and the bits that were added on as an afterthought. The later chapters especially felt like they lacked that sort of mental compactification that cohesifies everything under one vision. I'm sad because this could have been a phenominal work, and it's clear that a lot of effort was made, especially into interviews and data collection, and it feels like it's just lacking that one last missing piece of insight to bring it all the way home. So how much LLMs is too much LLMs? Well, when it comes to human connection, I'd say the answer is near zero. I don't want to read your AI generated e-mails, and I certainly don't want to read your AI generated essays. I'd much rather read your prompt instead, because I care about what you, yes, you personally think about, and I want to understand what you wanted to communicate. Don't get me wrong, I love LLMs for the right purpose. I'd love to use LLMs on doctor's notes to build models that predict whether the flu is spreading. But when it comes to writing, especially this kind of writing, it just feels so unnecessary, because when you write down your thoughts, I already have exactly what I wanted, and it just feels so silly to add an extra stop in between. As a poker player and game theorist, I'm sure Nate would appreciate the phrase "If you couldn't be bothered to write it, then I can't be bothered to read it". And you know, despite a belief that art can live separately from the artist, deep down for me this claim rings true. Not that the same words produced by a person are inherently different than the same words from an LLM, but it throws off my little Bayesian estimator a little. If the smartest person I know spent 10,000 hours writing, editing, polishing, and publishing a 500 page novel, it tells me not just that the smartest person I know had some thoughts on a topic, but it tells me that they decided to spend 10,000 hours of their precious time, and of their precious energy to communicate this idea to me. It feels good that the time it took me to read it is porportional (and usually less than) the time it took you to write it, because it shows me that you care about the time and energy of creating this exchange. And it's not just fully AI generated slop that hits this barrier. When you incorporate LLMs into your writing, even a little bit, you miss out on the ability to process your thoughts and create human connection.
